extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy/ethics; readers of classical moral theory
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Aristotle's evaluative standards for justice, voluntariness, equity, and intellectual/moral excellence as presented in Book V–VI of the Nicomachean Ethics. The page gives criteria for what counts as just/unjust action, character formation, equity, and the intellectual virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice as a mean
rubrics_metrics.description: Just acting is a mean between acting unjustly and being acted unjustly towards; Justice is a mean state which aims at producing the mean, whereas Injustice occupies both extremes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat justice not merely as conformity to law but as the disposition aimed at the appropriate mean between excess and defect in dealings. Example/implication: one who has 'more' or 'less' than the mean is involved in injustice; aim for proportionate balance rather than extremes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice as a moral state enabling proportionate division
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice is the moral state by virtue of which a person has the aptitude for practising the Just in moral choice and for making division between himself and another (or between two others) so as to give proportionably equal shares of what is choice-worthy and of what is hurtful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging distributions or adjudications, measure whether allocation respects proportional equality rather than absolute equality or mere favoritism. The just agent judges and allocates with regard to proportion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injustice defined by violation of proportion
rubrics_metrics.description: Injustice is excess or defect of what is good or hurtful respectively, in violation of the proportionate; Injustice aims at producing excess or defect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify injustice where actions or allocations intentionally produce disproportional advantage or disadvantage. Injustice involves intentional deviation from proportion (either gaining more or causing others to have less).

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntariness as condition for just/unjust action
rubrics_metrics.description: An action is just or unjust only when it is voluntary; involuntary or ignorant acts do not constitute just or unjust action except accidentally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating moral responsibility, first determine voluntariness. If an agent lacked control, knowledge, or was compelled, classify the action as involuntary/accidental for purposes of moral judgment and character-formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of voluntary action (knowledge and absence of compulsion)
rubrics_metrics.description: By 'voluntary' is meant what a person does with knowledge and with absence of ignorance as to the person hurt, the instrument, and the likely result, and not under compulsion—i.e. it rests with him to do or not to do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these tests: did the agent know whom he acted against, what means he used, and the probable result? Was the agent free from external compulsion? Examples: if another seizes one's hand and one strikes, the owner of the hand did not act voluntarily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctions among misadventure, mistake, and excusable ignorance
rubrics_metrics.description: When harm occurs contrary to reasonable expectation because of external causes it is a 'Misadventure'; when it occurs without viciousness but originates with the actor it is a 'Mistake'. Errors due to ignorance may be excusable; errors due to passions not attributable to infirmity may not be excused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify non-intentional harms by their origin: external unforeseeable events (misadventure) vs actor-originated errors (mistake). Use these distinctions when assessing blameworthiness and excuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate choice required for moral character formation
rubrics_metrics.description: A person may do unjust acts from impulse or passion without thereby having formed an unjust character; only when actions arise from deliberate choice does the doer become a confirmed unjust (or just) person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate repeated deliberate choices to determine character. Acts from transient passions (e.g., anger) can be unjust actions but need not indicate a vicious character unless chosen deliberately and knowingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Being unjustly dealt with requires absence of consent
rubrics_metrics.description: To be 'unjustly dealt with' the hurt must be against the wish of the sufferer; one cannot be unjustly dealt with with one's own consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing whether someone has been wronged, verify whether the suffering was against their will. Voluntary giving up of rights or property does not constitute being unjustly dealt with.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility for unjust distribution rests with the distributor
rubrics_metrics.description: In cases of distribution, it is the distributor who acts unjustly if he knowingly gives a larger share to one party contrary to the proper rate; the receiver who takes more does not thereby act unjustly in the same sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign blame to the originator of the unjust act (the person who makes the unfair award) rather than to a passive recipient, especially where voluntariness and knowledge originate with the distributor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity corrects the defects of universal law
rubrics_metrics.description: Equity (the Equitable) is Justice and is better than one form of Just (the strict letter of written law) because it corrects cases where universal legal statements fail to apply rightly; it is a 'correction of law where law is defective by reason of its universality.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a universal law leads to an unjust result in a particular case, apply equitable judgment that a lawgiver would make if present and informed of the exception. The equitable agent may waive strict legal claims to achieve just outcomes in exceptional cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural versus conventional justice
rubrics_metrics.description: Some forms of Justice are natural (having the same force everywhere and not dependent on reception), while others are conventional (dependent on human enactment and varying by place and custom).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between rules that claim universal moral force and those that are human conventions or decrees (e.g., prices, sacrificial practice). Evaluate whether a rule's authority is natural or contingent when applying justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social justice presupposes law, equality of ruling and being ruled
rubrics_metrics.description: Social (political) Justice arises among those who live in communion aiming at independence and are free and equal either proportionately or numerically; Just implies mutually acknowledged law and thus the possibility of injustice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the label 'social justice' to relations among equals under law; domestic relations (master/father/child/slave) involve different forms of justice because ownership and non-independence alter the possibility and meaning of injustice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unjust action must be voluntary, deliberate, and aggressive (not mere requital)
rubrics_metrics.description: An unjust action is one done voluntarily, of deliberate purpose, and aggressive (hurting without rightful requital). Hurts done in merely requiting a prior hurt are not thought to be unjust in the same way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing wrongdoing, require evidence of deliberation and aggression. Acts of retaliation or self-defence alter culpability and may not count as unjust in this sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: A person cannot deal unjustly with himself in the social-political sense
rubrics_metrics.description: Injustice presupposes plurality; one cannot be unjust to oneself in the sense of social injustice (e.g., one cannot seduce one's own wife, steal one's own property, or adjudicate against oneself as a form of public injustice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve the concept of doing social injustice for interactions between distinct persons or parties; self-directed harms may be blameworthy but are not social injustice by Aristotle's account (though community may still be harmed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice pertains to beings for whom proportion matters (primarily men)
rubrics_metrics.description: The province of Justice is among beings who can have too much or too little of goods and evils (i.e., humans); there may be beings (gods or incurably wicked) to which justice does not apply in the same way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply justice-based evaluations primarily to human social agents; recognize limits of the concept when applied to supernatural beings or those beyond benefit from justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral choice requires intellect and will aligned (Right Reason)
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral Choice is will consequent on deliberation; moral virtue is a state apt to exercise Moral Choice, which requires both a true Intellectual operation and the right Will. 'Right Reason' determines the mean and must be explicitly articulated for practical guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate moral action by checking whether intellect (deliberation about possible futures) and appetition/will are properly aligned toward the right end. Knowing what is just is not enough; one must be disposed and deliberate to act accordingly. The 'mean' must be specified by Right Reason rather than left vague.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual excellences distinguished and defined (knowledge, art, practical wisdom, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Intellectual virtues include Art, Knowledge, Practical Wisdom, Science, and Intuition; Knowledge pertains to what cannot be otherwise (necessities), is demonstrable syllogistically, eternal, and teachable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing intellectual excellence, use functional criteria: the excellence of a faculty is its state in which it best achieves its function (e.g., Knowledge is judged by syllogistic demonstration and teachability; Practical Wisdom by right deliberation about what can be otherwise).
